items.followUp: Describe the light reactions of photosynthesis and summarize how carbon dioxide is converted into carbohydrates in the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: The answer identifies the light reactions and their location.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they require light and occur in the thylakoids or grana of chloroplasts.

rubric.why: The answer identifies the dark reactions and their role in carbon fixation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they occur in the stroma and use products of the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide; they do not require light directly.

rubric.why: This is the initial carbon-fixation step of the cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that carbon dioxide combines with RuBP and forms an unstable six-carbon compound that splits into PGA.

rubric.why: This describes the reduction stage using energy and reducing power from the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ATP and NADPH are used to convert PGA into PGAL or G3P.

rubric.why: The cycle produces carbohydrates and regenerates its carbon dioxide acceptor.
rubric.description: Describes product formation and RuBP regeneration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that some PGAL forms sugars/carbohydrates and the remainder is used to regenerate RuBP.

modelAnswer: Light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes (grana) and require light; they produce ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from the splitting of water.
Dark reactions (the Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma. They do not require light directly and use ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP, forming an unstable six-carbon compound that splits into two molecules of PGA.
ATP and NADPH reduce PGA to PGAL (G3P).
Some PGAL is used to form sugars, while the rest regenerates RuBP.

items.followUp: Define a population and a community, and give an example of a community.

rubric.why: A community consists of populations of different species living together in an area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying different species or populations living together in the same area.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates a community of organisms in one habitat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as a pond or forest community.

modelAnswer: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
Example: a pond community, containing organisms such as fish, algae and insects.

items.followUp: What is exocytosis? Name its two main types.

rubric.why: Endocytosis brings material into a cell by enclosing it with the cell membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cell membrane enclosing material and bringing it into the cell.

rubric.why: These are the two types of endocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both phagocytosis and pinocytosis.

modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the process by which a cell takes substances in when its membrane surrounds them and forms a vesicle.
Its types are phagocytosis and pinocytosis.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis do homologous chromosomes separate, and what happens then?

rubric.why: Synapsis takes place during zygotene of prophase I.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying zygotene (prophase I) of meiosis.

rubric.why: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes along their lengths.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that homologous chromosomes pair along their lengths to form bivalents.

modelAnswer: Synapsis occurs during the zygotene stage of prophase I of meiosis.
Homologous chromosomes pair along their lengths, forming bivalents.

items.followUp: Differentiate between benign and malignant tumours.

rubric.why: Benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or spread to other tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that benign tumours are non-cancerous/localized and do not invade or spread.

rubric.why: Malignant tumours invade tissues and may spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that malignant tumours are cancerous and invade or spread to other tissues.

modelAnswer: Benign tumours are non-cancerous growths that remain localized and do not invade or spread to other tissues.
Malignant tumours are cancerous growths that invade nearby tissues and can spread to other parts of the body (metastasize).

items.followUp: Compare mitosis and meiosis by stating the number of divisions and the cells produced.

rubric.why: Mitosis has one division and meiosis has two divisions, producing different numbers of cells.
rubric.description: Compares the divisions and number of daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting one division/two daughter cells in mitosis with two divisions/four daughter cells in meiosis.

rubric.why: Mitosis maintains chromosome number, whereas meiosis halves it.
rubric.description: Compares the chromosome number and nature of cells produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis produces genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number, while meiosis produces haploid cells with half the chromosome number.

modelAnswer: Mitosis involves one cell division and produces two genetically identical daughter cells; meiosis involves two divisions and produces four daughter cells.
Mitosis maintains the chromosome number (usually diploid), whereas meiosis halves it and produces haploid cells.

items.followUp: Define a co-enzyme and name two examples.

rubric.why: A co-enzyme is an organic, non-protein helper molecule needed for enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a co-enzyme as an organic non-protein molecule that assists an enzyme.

rubric.why: NAD, FAD and co-enzyme A are examples of co-enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two valid examples.

modelAnswer: A co-enzyme is a small organic, non-protein molecule that assists an enzyme in carrying out its function.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme’s active site interacts with its substrate.

rubric.why: The substrate is the reactant on which an enzyme acts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the substrate as the substance or reactant acted upon by an enzyme.

rubric.why: The active site is the specific region where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site as the region of the enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs.

modelAnswer: A substrate is the substance or reactant on which an enzyme acts.
The active site is the specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
